Whether the pardon instrument is a full pardon is a legal reading of a document LegalEase does not see. The packet asks the participant what their document says and routes to counsel on anything other than a plain full pardon, but the characterisation should be reviewed before release.

Whether more than one felony conviction may be expunged within a single ten-year period, and on what showing each must independently qualify. The review states it is permitted where each is independently eligible under Article 978, and the current text does not address the point expressly.

Whether Article 985.3 displaces the Article 977(A)(2) five-year and Article 978(A)(2) ten-year waiting periods for a person who is otherwise eligible and has successfully completed a court-ordered probation or alternative sentencing programme. The word 'immediate' and the completion trigger suggest it does, but unlike Article 985.1(D) — which disapplies those time limitations in terms — Article 985.3 says nothing about them, and 'otherwise eligible for an expungement' can be read either as eligible but for the waiting period or as eligible including the waiting period. The difference decides who the eligibility engine returns.

Whether a charge dismissed after successful completion of a deferred disposition under 17-A M.R.S. ch. 67 subch. 4 is confidential criminal history record information under 16 M.R.S. § 703(2). This was checked against current official text and is NOT ESTABLISHED. Section 703(2) lists paragraphs A through L and none mentions a deferred disposition. The closest is paragraph G, which reaches a charge 'dismissed with prejudice by the court or dismissed with finality by a prosecutor outside a plea agreement'. Under 17-A M.R.S. § 1903 the State dismisses the charging instrument WITH PREJUDICE on compliance, which fits the first clause, but a deferred disposition arises from a written agreement between the defendant and the State, which arguably falls inside paragraph G's outside-a-plea-agreement carve-out. Section 1903 says nothing about confidentiality or sealing. No statute, State Bureau of Identification guidance, Judicial Branch page or Law Court decision resolves it. The packet therefore fails closed: it does not promise confidentiality on the strength of the deferred-disposition label, it tells the participant to verify what the Bureau record actually shows, and it routes the correction request only where the record is demonstrably inaccurate.

Form CR-308 page 2 carries a warning box stating that if at any time after the date of the order the defendant is convicted of a new crime in Maine or in any other jurisdiction, the new conviction extinguishes the order. That is inconsistent with 15 M.R.S. § 2264(7) as amended by PL 2025, c. 513, which now provides in terms that the subsection does not apply to records sealed pursuant to section 2262-A or 2262-B. Both the form and the amendment take effect 29 July 2026, so this is a live conflict on the face of two current official sources rather than a stale-form problem. LegalEase does not resolve it: the packet states the statutory rule, does not repeat the form's warning as advice, and carries the conflict as a release blocker.

How a participant with cases charged in more than one Missouri county obtains complete relief. § 610.140.2(2) requires every crime sought to be expunged to be listed in the one petition, while § 610.140.2(1) fixes venue by the court where the person was charged or found guilty; the two cannot both be satisfied across counties. The review records multi-county records as a referral trigger and the track treats it as a hard self-help stop rather than resolving it.

Whether a participant may invoke § 610.145.1(2) where the prosecutor or judicial officer who ordered the dismissal did not give the required notice. The subsection imposes a duty on them and gives the participant no mechanism to enforce it; the practical answer is to petition under subdivision (1) instead, which the packet does, but whether any lesser step — a letter to the prosecutor, a request to the clerk — is the expected course is not addressed anywhere in the section.

N.D.C.C. § 39-08-01.6(1) says the court shall seal, and states no motion or petition trigger, whereas the neighbouring marijuana provision says expressly upon motion. The petition requirement therefore rests on the official ND Courts research guide rather than on the statutory text, and participant copy must not represent the petition as statutorily mandated.

The exclusion of impaired-driving offences from Chapter 12-60.1 appears only in the official ND Courts research guides and not in the statutory exclusions at N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-02(2), which list only violence-or-intimidation felonies inside the firearm-disability period and registration offences. The routing to the separate § 39-08-01.6 seal follows the official guides, but the basis should be confirmed before release.

Whether venue is the district court of the county of arrest or any district court. The review states the county of arrest; the statutory text says only the district court. This must be closed before release.
Whether a motor vehicle offence under the Nebraska Rules of the Road reaches ordinance-level traffic offences, which would materially widen the mandatory-denial ground.

How the § 22-5-930(A) route interacts with § 44-53-450(b) for a participant who would now be eligible for a conditional discharge. Subsection (A) was read at source on 2026-08-06 and expressly includes 'those charges for which the person would now be eligible for a conditional discharge pursuant to Section 44-53-450', which brings some conditional-discharge-type facts inside the conviction route; subsection (D) separately bars the route where the person actually had a conditional discharge within the lookback period. Which route a participant with both features should be pointed to, and in what order, is a counselling question the statute does not answer.

How the § 61-11-26a(a)(1) 90-day single-misdemeanour clock interacts with the § 61-11-26(b)(1) one-year clock where the participant relies on job readiness graduation rather than 90 days of treatment compliance. Subdivision (a)(1) was read at source on 2026-08-06 and makes eligibility turn on '90 days' of programme compliance 'or upon completion of an approved job readiness adult training course, or both, if applicable, but after the completion of any sentence of incarceration or completion of any period of supervision, whichever is later in time'. On the graduation branch there is no stated period at all beyond completion of sentence and supervision, which would make the route available immediately on graduation. The packet applies the text as written and records the question rather than reading a 90-day period into the graduation branch.

Venue on a multi-county conviction petition. The controlling review states that S.B. 562 (2020) allows a person seeking expungement of convictions in more than one county to file in his or her county of residence. Section 61-11-26 was read in full at source on 2026-08-06 and the current text does not contain a residence-county venue option: subsections (a)(1) and (a)(2) both say 'petition the circuit court in which the conviction or convictions occurred', the subsection (d) proviso requires a multiple-misdemeanour petition to 'identify and group such information by circuit court, as applicable', and § 61-11-26a(a) says 'may petition the circuit court or circuit courts in which the conviction or convictions occurred'. Read together the current text supports one petition covering several counties, grouped by circuit court and served on the prosecuting attorney of each county of conviction, but it does not name a residence-county forum. Venue for the single-county case is unaffected and unambiguous. Until counsel resolves this, the packet directs a multi-county participant to the circuit court of conviction and adds a local-check instruction rather than promising a residence-county filing.

Where a multiple-misdemeanour group spans more than one county, which circuit court receives the single petition. Section 61-11-26 was read in full at source on 2026-08-06: subsection (a)(1) says 'the circuit court in which the conviction or convictions occurred', and the subsection (d) proviso requires the petition to 'identify and group such information by circuit court, as applicable'. Together those support one petition covering several counties, but the text does not say which of the several circuit courts is the forum, and it does not contain the county-of-residence option the controlling review attributes to S.B. 562. Until counsel answers, the packet directs the participant to the circuit court of conviction and, for a genuinely multi-county group, to a lawyer.

Whether an excluded conviction sitting inside an otherwise eligible multiple-misdemeanour group can be severed, so the remaining convictions are expunged, or whether its presence in the petition risks the whole petition being summarily denied under § 61-11-26(i)(4). The burden at subsection (h)(1) is framed per conviction, which suggests severance, but the once-per-lifetime rule makes the downside of getting it wrong permanent.

Whether § 5-1-16a(b) is the whole of the effect of a pardon expungement. The subsection was read at source on 2026-08-06 and provides only that the expunged record may not be considered in an application to a West Virginia educational institution or in an application for a licence required by a West Virginia professional organisation. Unlike §§ 61-11-25(e) and 61-11-26(l), it contains no general non-disclosure provision and no statement that the proceedings are considered never to have occurred. What the packet may tell a participant about disclosing the record to an ordinary employer after a § 5-1-16a expungement is therefore not settled.

questions.question: Whether a charge dismissed after successful completion of a deferred disposition under 17-A M.R.S. ch. 67 subch. 4 is confidential criminal history record information under 16 M.R.S. § 703(2).
